limitations: Retrospective design; the authors say the subtype-outcome findings should be confirmed prospectively before translation into guidelines
Diagnosis of adenoma remains challenging even for liver pathologists; only 87% of initial diagnoses were confirmed on review and 18 of 96 cases stayed borderline
Genotype-phenotype correlation was restricted to one representative nodule per patient and to non-necrotic, non-haemorrhagic areas
critique: Entirely a surgical series: every tumour was resected or transplanted, so subtype frequencies and the 46% HCC figure in beta-catenin tumours describe operated lesions, not the population of adenomas that exist
Inclusion required a prior suspicion of adenoma, and 9 cases were only 'possible' - circularity between the index diagnosis and the classification being derived from it
The association of beta-catenin with malignancy is cross-sectional: HCC was present at resection, not observed to develop, so this is co-occurrence rather than demonstrated transformation

Mean tumour diameter was 74-81 mm across every group; the series contains almost no small lesions, so it cannot speak to subtype behaviour below 5 cm even though the subtypes it defines are now used to decide management of small lesions

The size-haemorrhage association was significant only in non-HNF1A tumours and only for microscopic plus clinical bleeding pooled; the paper is nonetheless widely cited as general support for a size threshold
Mutation screening covered HNF1A, CTNNB1 and AXIN1 only; IL6ST, GNAS and the sonic hedgehog pathway were unknown, so the 'non-mutated inflammatory' group is defined by what was not looked for
No follow-up: the recommendation that beta-catenin patients 'could be closely followed' is not supported by any outcome data in the paper
16496320.bottom_line: Establishes that HCA is not one disease but at least four genotype-phenotype groups with very different association with malignancy, and incidentally shows that size does not predict haemorrhage in the HNF1A subtype - but it is a resection series of large tumours with no follow-up, so it defines subtypes without establishing their natural history.
16496320.funding: Association pour la Recherche sur le Cancer (ARC 3108), INSERM, Fondation de France; doctoral fellowships from Ligue Nationale Contre le Cancer and ARC. 'Potential conflict of interest: nothing to report.'

limitations: Retrospective multicentre review with non-standardised management across centres
The authors concede that patients with very small adenomas were not resected and were therefore excluded, so small lesions are under-represented
Only 5 malignancies, which the authors note precludes meaningful risk-factor analysis for malignancy
critique: The paper is the usual citation for 'no adenoma under 5 cm ruptures', but that is a post hoc observation in a cohort whose mean tumour size was around 8 cm and from which small lesions were explicitly excluded - the statement describes the sampling frame, not a tested threshold

Where a threshold was actually fitted, it fell at 7 cm; and the authors' own recommendation, 4 cm, matches neither their fitted cut-point nor the 5 cm observation, so three different numbers appear in one paper and the one that entered guidelines is the one with the least statistical support
Ascertainment is circular: rupture is what brings a patient to surgery, so a surgical series over-samples ruptured and large lesions and cannot estimate the rupture risk of an unselected adenoma
The 7 cm odds ratio has a confidence interval from 2.22 to 26.32 - the point estimate is unstable and compatible with effects an order of magnitude apart
No competing-risk or time-to-event analysis: rupture is treated as a prevalent state at presentation rather than an incidence over follow-up, so no annual risk can be derived
Dichotomising a continuous variable at a data-driven cut-point without correction inflates the apparent effect and the significance of the chosen threshold
Hormone use, the other independent predictor, is modifiable and was not pursued as an alternative to resection
19130136.bottom_line: The most frequently cited source for the 5 cm rule, which in fact fitted its size threshold at 7 cm, recommended resecting above 4 cm, and reached the '<5 cm never ruptures' observation in a cohort from which small adenomas had been deliberately excluded - so it supports the existence of a size effect but is the weakest possible foundation for the specific number in use.

limitations: Single-centre surgical series under a systematic resection policy, which the authors acknowledge limits generalisability
Retrospective design with no follow-up of unresected lesions
Small numbers of malignancies, limiting multivariable analysis
critique: The size gradient is an artefact of the denominator: the sub-2 cm stratum consists almost entirely of incidental microadenomas discovered inside specimens removed for a different, larger lesion, whereas the over-5 cm stratum consists of the lesions that prompted the operation - the two strata are not comparable populations

Counting lesions rather than patients inflates the small-lesion denominator enormously (365 adenomas in 122 patients), mechanically driving down the complication rate in the small strata; this per-lesion versus per-patient conflation is the single biggest statistical problem in the literature supporting the 5 cm rule
Microscopic haemorrhage found only because the specimen was removed and sectioned is an endpoint that cannot occur in a lesion left in situ; using it to justify resection is circular
A systematic resection policy means the indication for surgery was not size, so the cohort cannot tell us what a watched 4 cm or 6 cm adenoma does
Macroscopic haemorrhage in 24% of lesions over 5 cm is a prevalence at the time of resection, not an incidence, so no per-year risk can be derived for a surveillance decision

The one malignancy under 5 cm is reported only as '2-5 cm, exact size not presented', and it was in a man on steroids - the very group the guidelines already treat separately, so this paper's own data are consistent with size being irrelevant once sex and androgen exposure are accounted for
No multivariable analysis adjusting size for sex, subtype or hormone exposure, so the size effect is never separated from the factors that travel with it
19664629.bottom_line: The strongest-looking size gradient in the literature for both haemorrhage and malignancy, and the origin of the resect-all-men rule - but it is a per-lesion analysis in a resect-everything surgical series whose small-lesion denominator is made up of incidental microadenomas, so the gradient it displays is largely a property of how the lesions were counted.
19664629.funding: No funding statement. 'The authors disclose no conflicts.'

limitations: The authors state that a true size-based risk analysis was not possible because most studies reported only mean adenoma size and no study has specifically examined size against transformation
They note most included series were small, reported only resected adenomas, and may overestimate the true risk through selection and publication bias
They state that men with steroid-induced adenomas containing malignant foci are more likely to be published than uncomplicated cases, so 4.2% should be read as an upper limit
They call for a multicentre registry, saying the actual risk of malignant transformation cannot be established from the available literature
critique: The 4.2% figure that anchors most guideline statements on malignant risk is a crude aggregate of 174 heterogeneous publications spanning 40 years with no quality assessment, no weighting and no confidence interval; the authors say so, but the number travels without the caveat

The denominators are inconsistent within the paper itself: the abstract says 1635 adenomas, Table 1 totals 1617 and the discussion states 'a total of 1568 reported HCAs were found' - three different denominators for the headline rate

The '4.4% of transformations occurred below 5 cm' statistic is widely misread as a risk; it is a proportion of the numerator, not of the population, and says nothing about the probability that a sub-5 cm adenoma transforms

Three sub-5 cm transformations out of 68 is also a function of how few sub-5 cm adenomas were in the pooled denominator at all, since 89% of lesions were resected and small lesions are generally not resected - the comparison is unbalanced in the direction that favours the threshold
Case reports and series are pooled into a single rate, which guarantees an inflated numerator since case reports are published because transformation occurred
Excluding glycogen storage disease and adenomatosis is defensible but means the pooled rate does not apply to two of the populations in which guidelines most often invoke malignant risk

Of the three sub-5 cm transformations, one was in a man on steroids and one in a 53-year-old man - so the paper's own counter-examples to the threshold are concentrated in the group already exempt from it
Published 2010, before molecular subtyping, so beta-catenin status - now the dominant predictor - is absent from every pooled analysis
20887318.n: 174 articles (157 series, 17 case reports) covering 1635 hepatocellular adenomas; 1617 in series, of which 1445 (89%) resected
20887318.bottom_line: The source of the canonical 4.2% malignant transformation figure and of the '4.4% occurred below 5 cm' statistic, both of which are crude aggregates of 174 unappraised publications with three mutually inconsistent denominators - and the authors themselves conclude that the 5 cm treatment recommendation is 'open for debate' and that over 95% of resections above it are unnecessary.
20887318.funding: No funding statement. 'Conflicts of interest: none declared.'

limitations: The authors describe the series as small and unique and state that additional data from multiple centres are needed
They say prognostic factors for rupture and malignant degeneration during pregnancy remain unknown
Imaging frequency was not standardised, depending on lesion size and change
Literature on the course of HCA during pregnancy is scarce because of the rarity of the condition
critique: Twelve patients with no rupture cannot support the safety claim the paper advances: zero events in 17 pregnancies has an upper 95% bound of roughly 20%, so the data are compatible with a clinically unacceptable risk

The cohort was pre-selected by the institutional policy: adenomas of 5 cm or more that did not regress were treated before pregnancy, so the women who reached pregnancy were those already judged low-risk - the good outcome partly measures the success of that filtering, not the safety of pregnancy with an adenoma
Two of the 12 patients had been operated and one embolised before pregnancy, so the series does not describe untreated adenoma in pregnancy

The one patient with substantial growth became pregnant a second time against advice and again needed a preterm caesarean - a single patient generating two of the three caesareans, which the per-pregnancy denominator obscures

The historical comparator (44% maternal mortality) comes from 26 published case reports of women presenting acutely, the most biased possible control, so the apparent improvement conflates better selection, better imaging and publication bias

Growth is reported as a count without a definition of significant growth or a measurement-reproducibility estimate, and the key case's 32 to 75 mm change was measured on different sequences years apart
12 of 183 database patients became pregnant and were monitored, so the denominator excludes women who conceived and were not referred back - the loss is in the direction that would hide complications
No subtype data, although sonic hedgehog and beta-catenin exon 7/8 adenomas are the ones that bleed small and would be the relevant risk group in a pregnancy decision
21094555.n: 12 women followed through 17 pregnancies (12 of 183 HCA patients in the database)
21094555.bottom_line: The series that began the shift away from advising against pregnancy in hepatocellular adenoma, reporting 17 uneventful pregnancies with growth in four and no rupture - but with twelve patients pre-filtered by a policy of treating lesions over 5 cm beforehand, it cannot establish the safety it proposes, only that a wait-and-see approach is reasonable in small adenomas.
21094555.funding: No funding. 'The authors who have taken part in this study declare that they do not have anything to disclose regarding funding or conflict of interest.'

limitations: Single-centre retrospective series with referral bias towards complex and malignant cases
The authors note that diagnosing adenoma-derived HCC requires residual adenoma in the specimen, so the frequency of adenoma behind a fully developed HCC is underestimated
Beta-catenin status could not be assessed in every case
critique: 47% transformation in men is the number that justifies resecting every male adenoma, but its denominator is the small number of men in a tertiary surgical series - men with large or suspicious lesions are preferentially referred and operated, so this is close to a maximum, not a population risk

The subsequent finding that half of presumed male adenomas are not adenomas at all (Furumaya 2021) means the 47% may partly measure misclassification of HCC as transformed adenoma rather than true transformation

The three sub-5 cm transformations all occurred in abnormal background liver, which argues that background fibrosis or iron overload rather than size is the discriminating feature - but this is three cases and cannot support a rule either way

Transformation is ascertained on the resection specimen, so larger lesions, being more extensively sampled and more often resected, are more likely to yield a malignant focus - verification bias aligned with the size finding

Beta-catenin activation in 64% of transformed cases is presented without the corresponding prevalence in non-transformed adenomas in the same cohort, so no relative risk can be computed from the paper as reported
Cross-sectional co-occurrence throughout: nothing was followed over time, so no annual transformation hazard is derivable for a surveillance decision
21148580.bottom_line: The foundational evidence that malignant transformation of adenoma is overwhelmingly a male phenomenon (47% vs 4%) and is associated with beta-catenin activation and large size, and the basis for resecting all male adenomas - but it is a tertiary surgical series whose male denominator is small and whose diagnostic label has since been shown to be unreliable in men.
21148580.funding: No funding statement identified in the extracted text; flagged here as not established from the text rather than absent.

limitations: Immunohistochemistry was unavailable in 19% of biopsies because of insufficient material, which the authors attribute to the retrospective design and expect to be less of a problem prospectively
The improvement from adding immunohistochemistry should be 'tuned down' because the reading pathologist was a liver-tumour specialist; general pathologists would gain more
Biopsies were read once only, on the grounds that immunophenotypic subtyping is less observer-dependent and includes internal controls
critique: Only 47 of 167 operated patients qualified, selected on having had both tests in-house - a convenience subset whose referral route plausibly differs from the rest

Beta-catenin-activated HCA, the subtype that drives management, is effectively absent as a category: just three lesions showed beta-catenin activation and none was analysed as a separate subtype, so the study cannot tell us whether MRI or biopsy detects the subtype that matters most

72% telangiectatic/inflammatory is far above the usual one third, so accuracy figures are inflated by a prevalent, imaging-distinctive subtype; applying the same likelihood ratios in a case mix with more steatotic or beta-catenin lesions would yield worse performance
Unclassified HCA numbered 2, so the 50% sensitivity and LR 22.5 quoted for that group are uninterpretable

The reference standard is the resection specimen read at the same institution, and the subtyping rule gave morphology precedence over immunophenotype when they conflicted, so reference and test are not fully independent
Verification bias by design: only resected lesions can have a reference standard, so nothing is known about MRI accuracy in the small, unresected adenomas where subtyping would change management

The genuinely useful negative result - that accuracy is no worse below 5 cm - is reported in one sentence in the results and is not carried into the discussion or conclusion, even though it removes the main technical objection to subtype-based management of small lesions
21480324.n: 47 HCA nodules in 47 patients (41 women, 6 men)
21480324.bottom_line: Shows that MRI and biopsy each assign HCA subtype correctly about 80% of the time with excellent interobserver agreement, and - importantly for a pathway - that accuracy does not deteriorate in lesions under 5 cm; but it contains almost no beta-catenin-activated adenomas, so it does not establish that the subtype which should override size can be detected.
21480324.funding: No funding statement. 'Potential conflict of interest: nothing to report.'

limitations: Small retrospective single-centre series
The authors note heterogeneity in lesion size, number and ablation technique over the study period
Follow-up imaging intervals were not standardised
critique: A primary efficacy of 57.8% is a poor result for a procedure offered as an alternative to resection, and the percutaneous figure of 31% means the minimally invasive route - the only one that offers an advantage over surgery - failed two times in three
Per-lesion efficacy in 18 patients with 45 lesions means the denominator is inflated by multiple small lesions in the same patient; per-patient complete treatment is not reported and would be lower

Thirteen of eighteen patients were treated because they wished to become pregnant, but no pregnancy outcomes are reported, so the study does not establish that ablation achieved the purpose for which it was performed

Two major complications in 18 patients is a rate of roughly 11%, comparable to or worse than contemporary laparoscopic resection series, yet the paper is cited as evidence that ablation is the lower-risk option

No histology after ablation, so the diagnosis cannot be confirmed and a malignant focus cannot be excluded - the central objection to any ablative approach in a lesion whose chief danger is malignant transformation
No comparator arm: all comparisons are internal between approaches
Published 2011, before molecular subtyping, so there is no way to know whether the ablated lesions were the ones that needed treating
21616431.bottom_line: The founding series for radiofrequency ablation of hepatocellular adenoma, showing primary efficacy of only 57.8% overall and 31% percutaneously with two major complications in eighteen patients - so it establishes feasibility rather than a credible alternative to resection, and leaves no tissue to confirm the diagnosis.
21616431.funding: No funding statement identified in the extracted text; flagged here as not established from the text rather than absent.

limitations: The authors state that the included studies are predominantly surgical series and that the pooled rates should therefore be read as maximum rather than true risks
Heterogeneous definitions of haemorrhage and rupture across the 28 articles
Size was reported in only 13 of 28 articles, preventing a pooled size-stratified analysis
No meta-analytic pooling with confidence intervals was performed; figures are simple aggregates
critique: This review contains the most direct refutation of the threshold available - 6 of 13 size-reporting articles documented bleeding below 5 cm, with the smallest at 1 cm - yet it is routinely cited for its headline 27.2% bleeding rate, which the authors themselves disown as a maximum
With 91.2% of the pooled patients resected, the entire evidence base for 'how often adenomas bleed' is an operated population; the unoperated adenoma has essentially never been counted

The per-patient (27.2%) versus per-lesion (15.8%) discrepancy means every downstream citation must specify which denominator it means, and most do not - a 5 cm rule derived from per-lesion data and applied per patient is not the same rule

68.5% of bleeds being the presenting event implies that most haemorrhage is unpreventable by surveillance at any threshold, since the lesion was unknown until it bled; this undercuts the logic of prophylactic resection rather than relocating the threshold
Simple aggregation across 28 heterogeneous retrospective series with no weighting, no random-effects model and no confidence intervals; the precision implied by figures like 27.2% is spurious
Publication bias runs strongly towards reporting bleeding, which the review does not formally assess
No separation of histological from clinically significant haemorrhage across the pooled studies, so the 27.2% mixes incidental microscopic findings with life-threatening rupture
22619025.n: 28 articles, 1176 patients; haemorrhage denominators 1160 patients and 748 lesions
22619025.bottom_line: The reference systematic review on adenoma bleeding, which documents haemorrhage down to 1 cm, reports that two thirds of bleeds are the presenting event, and tells the reader explicitly that its 27.2% figure is a maximum derived from a 91% resected population - three findings that between them dismantle the empirical case for a 5 cm prophylactic threshold.
22619025.funding: No funding statement. 'The authors declare no conflict of interest.'

limitations: The number of adenomas with malignant transformation (16) is small, so the 44% figure is imprecise
The authors note that the mechanism by which the mutated promoter increases transcription required further work
critique: The 0/60 figure in typical adenomas is the paper's most quoted result for adenoma management, but 60 tumours gives an upper 95% confidence bound of about 5% - it cannot exclude a clinically relevant rate of TERT mutation in typical HCA
Cross-sectional: the ordering of CTNNB1 then TERT is inferred from co-occurrence in already-transformed lesions, not observed longitudinally
Tissue came from resection and transplant collections, so 'typical HCA' here means a resected adenoma - the specimens least likely to be left alone and watched
No size, sex or subtype breakdown of the 60 typical adenomas is given, so the result cannot be used to stratify risk within the adenoma population

A pathway that detects transformation only once it has occurred has no demonstrated prospective value: the paper supports TERT as a confirmatory marker, not as a screening or surveillance test, a distinction often lost in citation
23887712.n: 305 HCC, 20 cirrhotic macronodules, 16 HCA with malignant transformation, 60 typical HCA
23887712.bottom_line: Identifies TERT promoter mutation as the step that completes malignant transformation of beta-catenin-mutated adenomas and as the commonest somatic event in HCC, but with only 60 typical adenomas screened it provides a confirmatory marker of transformation rather than a tool for stratifying adenomas before it happens.
23887712.funding: INCa with the ICGC project, 'Reseau national CRB Foie', ARC 3194, NoFLIC, Ligue Nationale Contre le Cancer; authors declare no competing financial interests.

limitations: Retrospective single-centre design
The authors acknowledge that nearly half the lesions could not be assigned a molecular subtype, limiting subtype-stratified analysis
Bleeding was assessed on imaging and pathology of variable protocol over the study period
critique: The study set out to find a size threshold and found one at 35 mm - a full 15 mm below the convention it was implicitly testing; the number in the guidelines is therefore not the number that emerges when the question is asked directly

Fatally circular: the institution's own protocol used 5 cm to decide resection, so which lesions were removed, sectioned and had their bleeding characterised was determined by the very variable under test

Bleeding grades I to III are pooled in the headline 5.4% versus 53% comparison, so clinically trivial intratumoral blood is counted alongside peritoneal rupture; the threshold for the outcome that matters is not reported separately

Zero beta-catenin adenomas in 195 lesions is implausible against a literature prevalence of 10-20% and indicates that the subtyping was inadequate, which together with 48% unclassifiable means the study cannot exclude subtype as the real driver behind the apparent size effect
A data-derived cut-point reported without cross-validation, bootstrapping or correction for multiple thresholds tested; 35 mm is a best fit in this dataset, not a validated threshold
Per-lesion analysis with no accounting for multiple lesions in the same patient, so observations are not independent
Prevalence of bleeding at presentation, not incidence over time, so nothing here converts into a risk per year of surveillance
24760723.n: 195 hepatocellular adenomas (129 below and 66 above the 35 mm threshold)
24760723.bottom_line: The one study that set out explicitly to derive a bleeding threshold derived 35 mm rather than 50 mm - which is the clearest evidence that 5 cm is a convention rather than a measured cut-point - though its own protocol already used 5 cm to select which lesions were resected, and half its lesions were unsubtypeable.
24760723.funding: No funding statement. 'The authors declare no conflict of interest.'

limitations: The guideline states that its recommendations are expert opinion, there being insufficient evidence for formal grading
The authors note the rarity of GSD I prevents randomised or prospective comparative study of adenoma management
No validated surveillance interval or threshold is available for this population
critique: An expert-opinion guideline for a population in which adenoma is almost universal, written without any cohort data on when intervention helps - so GSD I patients are managed by extrapolation from cohorts of young women on oral contraceptives, a different disease biologically

That AFP and CEA are explicitly useless for surveillance leaves imaging size as the only monitored variable, which reimports the 5 cm convention into a population in which it was never tested and in which adenomas are multiple from adolescence

A mean presentation age of 14.8 years means these decisions are being made in children, where the cumulative burden of repeated imaging and the lifetime consequences of resection are greatest and least studied
Chromosome 6p gain/6q loss in 60% is reported as a molecular feature without any stated clinical use, so it describes rather than stratifies
The guideline predates the sonic hedgehog subtype and the exon-specific beta-catenin gradient, so its adenoma recommendations rest on a molecular picture now known to be incomplete
Progression in 50% is given without a time base, so it cannot be converted into a surveillance interval
No explicit recommendation grading system is applied to the adenoma sections, so a reader cannot distinguish the strength of one recommendation from another
25356975.bottom_line: The reference guideline for glycogen storage disease type I, establishing that hepatic adenomas affect 70-80% of adults with the condition from a mean age of 14.8 years and that tumour markers are useless for surveillance - but its adenoma recommendations are explicitly expert opinion, leaving a near-universal paediatric complication managed by convention borrowed from a different population.
25356975.funding: No funding statement for the guideline. 'The authors declare no conflict of interest.'

limitations: Retrospective registry study with heterogeneous practice across European centres and decades
The authors note that registry coding of the indication was unreliable, requiring manual verification
Incomplete molecular subtyping, reflecting the era of most transplants
critique: Three operative deaths plus three fatal HCC recurrences in 49 transplants means roughly one in eight patients died of the treatment or its failure - a mortality that must be set against the 2.5% ten-year transformation rate Barbier reports for adenomatosis managed conservatively

35% malignant transformation on explant is a selection artefact of the transplant indication: suspected malignancy is itself a reason to transplant, so this figure describes who gets listed, not what adenomatosis does

That 15 of 64 registry entries were miscoded is a serious finding about registry-based evidence in this disease generally, and it means other registry analyses of adenoma - including UNOS studies - should be read with the same scepticism
No denominator of patients with adenomatosis who were not transplanted, so no risk-benefit comparison is possible from this paper
Spans multiple decades of transplant practice with no era stratification, so outcomes mix pre-modern and contemporary immunosuppression and selection
Five retransplantations are reported without indication or timing, so graft loss cannot be attributed
Molecular subtype is largely absent, so the paper cannot say whether the transplanted patients were the beta-catenin-mutated group in whom radical treatment would be most defensible
26919265.n: 49 liver transplantations (64 initially identified in the registry)
26919265.bottom_line: The definitive European series of transplantation for adenomatosis, showing true malignant transformation in 35% of explants but three operative deaths, five retransplantations and three fatal recurrences - and, incidentally, that registry coding for adenoma is unreliable enough to require manual verification of a quarter of cases.
26919265.funding: No funding statement identified in the extracted text; flagged here as not established from the text rather than absent.

limitations: The guideline grades its two central adenoma recommendations at evidence level II-3 - non-randomised observational evidence - and recommendation strength 2, the weaker category, so it does not claim strong evidential support
It acknowledges the scarcity of prospective data on the natural history of untreated adenoma
It notes the difficulty of differentiating adenoma from focal nodular hyperplasia and from well-differentiated HCC on imaging alone
critique: The guideline's own language gives the game away: the threshold is described as the 'accepted clinically relevant size cut off', and its central factual premise - that nearly all ruptures occur at 5 cm or more - is supported by one citation, whereas the literature available in 2016 already contained Bieze's 35 mm threshold, van Aalten's bleeding at 1 cm and Deneve's fitted cut-point at 7 cm

A recommendation graded II-3 with strength 2 is, by the guideline's own scheme, weak observational evidence and a conditional recommendation - yet in practice it is applied as a bright-line rule, which is a failure of transmission the guideline did not cause but did not guard against
The 20% growth criterion is borrowed from RECIST, an oncological response framework designed for a different purpose in malignant disease, and no validation of it in benign tumours is cited

The recommendation against routine molecular subtyping conflicts directly with the evidence base the same European groups were generating: Nault's work shows subtype outperforms size for both outcomes, and this guideline forecloses the only measurement that would allow the threshold to be replaced
No decision analysis or explicit weighing of operative morbidity and mortality against the prevented events, so the threshold is stated without the cost side of the calculation

Resecting all adenomas in men at II-3 rests on Dokmak's and Farges's tertiary surgical series; the subsequent finding that half of male 'adenomas' are misdiagnosed is not something the 2016 guideline could have known but does invalidate its evidential basis

Two of the authors (Colombo and Zucman-Rossi) carry extensive industry disclosures; this is not obviously material to a size threshold, but the hepatobiliary-contrast imaging recommendation does have commercial beneficiaries
The guideline has not been updated despite Julien 2021 explicitly reporting that no threshold size could be identified
27085809.bottom_line: The document that fixed 5 cm into European practice, and which describes the number itself as the 'accepted' cut-off while grading the recommendation at II-3/strength 2 on a single-citation factual premise - so the pathway's claim that 5 cm is a convention rather than a derived threshold is supported by the guideline's own wording and grading.
27085809.funding: No external funding for the guideline stated. Author disclosures include extensive industry relationships for several panel members, notably Colombo and Zucman-Rossi.

limitations: The function of residues K335 and N387 in regulating beta-catenin remains unknown

The authors state that the role of S45 in physiological regulation and in tumorigenesis needs further investigation, as their low-activity finding contradicts the prevailing priming-phosphorylation model
A second hit remains unidentified in 30% of HCC with weak mutations and GLUL overexpression
S45-mutated adenomas show a GS pattern that is intense but heterogeneous and difficult to recognise, so the authors say IHC criteria must be revised or mutation screening performed
critique: Entirely a surgical series from tertiary referral centres, so the 25% CTNNB1 rate in adenomas and the activity distribution reflect operated tumours

The inference that exon 7/8 mutations carry low malignant risk is indirect - it rests on their rarity in HCC, not on any adenoma followed to transformation; no adenoma in this series was observed over time

Activity classes are defined by cross-sectional mRNA in tumours of different stages, so the 'just right' dosage model is a hypothesis fitted to prevalence data rather than a demonstrated selection process

Clinically, the paper undercuts the test that guidelines rely on: if only 27% of mutated adenomas show the textbook strong homogeneous GS pattern, any pathway that triages by GS immunohistochemistry alone will under-detect the subtype it is most trying to find, and the paper recommends sequencing that most centres do not perform
Size is not analysed against mutation type anywhere, so the finding most relevant to a 5 cm threshold - whether high-activity mutations cluster in large lesions - is simply absent
Borderline lesions number only 17, and 65% mutation plus 70% large deletions in that group rests on a handful of cases
No denominators are given for how many of the 220 adenomas had assessable GS and CD34 staining, so the sensitivity and specificity figures quoted downstream from this work come from small subsets
27177928.n: 610 hepatocellular tumours from 559 patients: 220 HCA, 373 HCC, 17 borderline HCA/HCC
27177928.bottom_line: Shows that malignant risk in beta-catenin-activated adenoma is graded by exactly which CTNNB1 residue is mutated, which is the strongest available argument for stratifying by subtype rather than size, but it also shows that routine glutamine synthetase staining identifies only a minority of mutated adenomas, so the stratification it recommends is not deliverable with the tools most centres use.

limitations: No limitations section
critique: Retrospective and exclusively surgical: every one of the 533 lesions was resected, so the denominators for bleeding and transformation are operated adenomas, which inflates both relative to the adenoma population at large

The paper is almost always cited for its subtype classification and almost never for the result that most constrains practice - that 50 mm predicts histologic but not symptomatic haemorrhage (P=0.29), the latter being the outcome surgery is meant to prevent
Size versus malignancy at P=0.053 is a null result at conventional thresholds, yet guidelines citing this paper treat size as an established malignancy risk factor

TERT promoter mutation with OR 67.6 and a confidence interval spanning 8.3 to 3072 reflects near-complete separation in a handful of events; it is diagnostically useful but statistically unstable, and TERT is by definition present only once transformation has occurred, so it cannot pre-empt it

The at-risk stratification in women <5 cm rests on 2 transformations among 14 women; it is a hypothesis-generating subgroup, not a validated rule, yet it is the only evidence offered anywhere for abandoning the size threshold in small lesions

Malignant transformation is defined on the resection specimen, so a lesion resected for being large is more likely to have its small malignant focus found - verification bias that works in the same direction as the size association being tested
Centrally reviewed by the group that devised the classification, with no external pathology adjudication
No prospective follow-up of unresected lesions, so nothing in the paper describes what happens to an adenoma that is watched

The sonic hedgehog subtype, the only one that predicts symptomatic bleeding, cannot be identified on imaging and needs molecular profiling, so the single actionable bleeding predictor in the paper is not available in the clinic where the 5 cm decision is made

Definitions of surgery avoidance and of complication severity differed across studies
Follow-up was limited, with a pooled median of 31 months

The senior author consults for Siemens, Medtronic and Interventional Systems, the last of which supplies the stereotactic navigation platform the technique depends on - a direct interest in the result
Single-operator, single-centre results with a highly specialised technique are the least transferable kind of interventional evidence, and the paper does not report a learning curve
No histological confirmation after ablation, so neither the diagnosis nor the exclusion of a malignant focus is established
Disease-free survival in a benign tumour is a borrowed oncological endpoint with no agreed definition here, and the drop from 100% to 85.8% is not explained in terms of what event occurred
The indication for treating these 38 adenomas is not analysed against guideline thresholds, so it is unknown whether any of them needed treatment at all
35654476.bottom_line: Shows that stereotactic multiprobe radiofrequency ablation achieves far better technical efficacy (97.4%) than conventional ablation with no major complications over four years of follow-up, but in only 14 patients, at a single specialised centre, with the senior author consulting for the navigation-platform manufacturer and no tissue to confirm what was ablated.
35654476.funding: No funding. Reto Bale consults for Siemens, Medtronic and Interventional Systems.

limitations: The panel grades the evidence behind every hepatocellular adenoma recommendation as very low quality (D) with conditional strength, bar two
It states that in beta-catenin-mutated adenoma in women the available data do not allow stratification by lesion size
It notes that most imaging studies overestimated MRI accuracy by failing to classify HCA subtypes, with possible misclassification of inflammatory adenoma as telangiectatic FNH
It records that identification of the beta-catenin subtype by imaging is impossible, and that about 10% of inflammatory adenomas have a mixed beta-catenin phenotype undetectable on imaging
It acknowledges no randomised trials exist comparing contraceptive continuation with discontinuation, only small case series and case reports
It states the natural course of liver adenomatosis is poorly described
critique: This guideline is the most useful document in the depot for auditing the threshold, because it applies GRADE honestly and the answer comes back 'very low quality, conditional' for every size-based recommendation - meaning the 5 cm rule has now been formally appraised by the most rigorous method applied to it and has failed

Having conceded that beta-catenin identification is impossible on imaging and that size cannot stratify risk in beta-catenin-mutated women, the guideline nonetheless retains a size-and-time rule as the operative recommendation, so its own reasoning does not reach its own conclusion

It recommends biopsy to find exon 3 and sonic hedgehog subtypes (PICO 9) and simultaneously keeps 5 cm as the resection trigger (PICO 11) without specifying which takes precedence when they conflict - the commonest real decision

The malignant-risk premise is Stoot's 4.2% and '4.4% below 5 cm', reproduced without the caveats Stoot himself states, and the 4.4% is again presented as though it were a risk rather than a proportion of the numerator

It cites Nault's 71% vs 14% symptomatic bleeding figure for sonic hedgehog adenoma but not Nault's finding in the same paper that 50 mm does not predict symptomatic bleeding (P=0.29) - selective extraction from the single most relevant study
Published in 2022, after Julien 2021 reported that no threshold size could be identified, and does not cite or address it

The surveillance schedule (6 months, 1 year, then annual ultrasound indefinitely) is graded D/conditional and is asserted without any event-rate analysis, so the interval is as conventional as the threshold

Seven societies including radiology, surgery, ultrasound and transplantation co-authored it; the recommendations that expand imaging, biopsy and operative activity are the ones retained despite the weakest grading
36089523.bottom_line: The only hepatocellular adenoma guideline built on a formal GRADE framework, and it grades every size-based recommendation - including the 5 cm resection trigger and the 6-month decision point - as very low quality evidence with conditional strength, while conceding that the beta-catenin subtype which determines risk cannot be seen on imaging and that size cannot stratify risk once it is known.
36089523.funding: No funding statement for the guideline. 'The Authors declare no conflict of interest.'

limitations: Retrospective and dependent on the completeness of national pathology and operative records
The authors note that preoperative imaging protocols were not standardised across the period and centres studied
Molecular subtyping was not uniformly available, so some reclassifications rest on morphology and immunohistochemistry alone
critique: This is the best available measurement of the cost of acting on the size threshold, yet it measures diagnostic error rather than harm: no operative morbidity, mortality or quality-of-life outcome is reported, so the price of the 20% of resections done below 50 mm is quantified only as a wrong label

A 43% change of diagnosis presupposes that the final pathology is right; without central re-review or molecular confirmation some of these 'changes' may be reclassification between equally uncertain categories rather than correction of error

The adjusted odds ratio of 1.8 for absence of hepatobiliary MRI is confounded by era and centre - lesions imaged without hepatobiliary agents were generally imaged earlier and in less specialised units, and those factors are not separable here
Numerators and denominators for the FNH finding are given as percentages only, so the 21% figure rests on roughly nine lesions
Selection is on having been resected, so the study cannot say how often the diagnosis is wrong in lesions that were watched - plausibly more often, which would strengthen its own argument
No analysis of whether the diagnostic change altered subsequent management or follow-up, so the clinical significance of the 43% is undetermined
36324268.n: 222 resections for presumed hepatocellular adenoma, 44 (20%) of lesions <50 mm
36324268.bottom_line: Quantifies the operational cost of a size-driven pathway: a fifth of Dutch resections for presumed adenoma were for lesions under 5 cm, 70% of those had their diagnosis changed afterwards and a fifth proved to be focal nodular hyperplasia - evidence that the problem with the threshold is not only where it sits but that the diagnosis it is applied to is often wrong.
36324268.funding: No funding statement identified in the extracted text; flagged here as not established from the text rather than absent.

limitations: 21% response rate, which the authors acknowledge limits representativeness
Self-reported practice rather than observed management
The authors note that respondents are likely to be those with the greatest interest in benign liver tumours
critique: A 21% response rate means 79% of invitees are unaccounted for, and the direction of that non-response is unknowable - clinicians who follow the guideline may have seen no need to reply, which would exaggerate the apparent dissent

Stated preference is not practice: the survey records what experts say they advise, with no audit of what they actually do, and the same group's own Dutch resection audit found 20% of resections performed below 50 mm

Respondents are self-selected enthusiasts at referral centres, so their willingness to depart from a size rule reflects access to subtyping and hepatobiliary MRI that general centres lack - the finding does not transfer

The question as reported conflates 'routine resection' with resection, so a respondent who resects selectively above 5 cm would answer against routine resection; the 79% figure may overstate the disagreement

That only half the respondents have a guideline-compliant multidisciplinary team is arguably the more consequential finding, since every subtype-based alternative to the threshold presupposes exactly that infrastructure - yet it is reported as a secondary result
No denominators by country, specialty or centre volume, so the sources of variation cannot be identified
Surveys cannot establish whether the majority view is correct; this is evidence about the standing of the threshold among experts, not about its validity
36781070.n: 61 analysable respondents of 294 invited (21% response rate)
36781070.bottom_line: Shows that four fifths of responding European experts decline to follow the EASL recommendation to resect adenomas remaining above 5 cm after lifestyle change, and that only half have the multidisciplinary infrastructure the guideline assumes - evidence that the threshold has lost consensus, though from a 21% response rate of self-selected specialists reporting stated rather than observed practice.
36781070.funding: No funding statement identified in the extracted text; flagged here as not established from the text rather than absent.

limitations: Small single-institution series, limiting subtype-specific conclusions
The authors note that molecular confirmation of beta-catenin status was not available in all cases, with subtyping resting on immunohistochemistry
Retrospective archival design with variable clinical follow-up
critique: With 27 adenomas and 4 transformations, every subtype-specific rate is based on single figures; the 14.8% transformation rate has a confidence interval wide enough to encompass most published estimates

A negative result for the study's own hypothesis (androgen receptor does not predict transformation) is reported without a power calculation, so the paper cannot distinguish no effect from an undetected one

That transformation occurred in unclassified as well as beta-catenin adenomas undercuts a subtype-only triage strategy, but with one or two cases it equally fails to establish that unclassified lesions are dangerous

25.9% unclassified is two to three times the rate in series using full molecular analysis, suggesting incomplete characterisation rather than a biologically distinct population - and the 'unclassified transforms' finding may therefore be an artefact of unperformed sequencing
Referral-based archival series at a tertiary centre: cases reach the file because they were difficult or dramatic, so neither the subtype mix nor the transformation rate generalises
No lesion sizes are related to transformation, so the series cannot inform the size question in men despite men being the group for whom size is already supposed to be irrelevant
37245629.n: 33 lesions in men: 27 hepatocellular adenomas and 6 hepatocellular neoplasms of uncertain malignant potential
37245629.bottom_line: A small archival series showing that malignant transformation of adenoma in men occurs in beta-catenin-inflammatory and unclassified subtypes and that androgen receptor staining does not predict it; too small to establish rates, but a reminder that a quarter of male adenomas remain unclassified and that transformation is not confined to the subtypes a pathway would flag.

limitations: The guideline grades the adenoma recommendations as conditional on low quality evidence
It acknowledges the absence of prospective comparative data on surveillance intervals and on the timing of resection
It notes the difficulty of distinguishing adenoma subtypes on imaging
critique: Published in 2024, it reproduces the 5 cm threshold and the 6-month decision point without engaging either Julien 2021 ('we did not identify a threshold size') or Klompenhouwer 2017 (only 8.5-15.3% regress below 5 cm by 6 months) - the two studies that most directly test what it recommends

The 6.5 cm pregnancy trigger is adopted from Haring's pooled case-report literature, where 6.5 cm is the smallest size among published haemorrhages rather than a derived threshold; a publication-limited minimum has become a treatment criterion in a GRADE guideline

Six-monthly imaging for two years then annually is a schedule with no stated evidential basis and no exit condition, committing young women to indefinite imaging - in contrast to the French guideline which at least permits stopping after menopause

Resecting all adenomas in men is retained despite the 2021 Dutch finding that half of male 'adenomas' are reclassified on expert review, which means the rule is applied to a diagnostic category known to be unreliable in exactly that group

GRADE is applied and returns 'conditional, low quality' for the central recommendations, but the recommendations themselves are worded as thresholds rather than as the conditional judgements the grading implies - the same transmission failure as in EASL

No decision-analytic comparison of resection against continued surveillance, despite now having contemporary surveillance outcome data (symptomatic bleeding 0.5%, transformation 0.8%) that would materially change the balance
Does not address what to do when imaging suggests a high-risk subtype in a lesion under 5 cm, which is the case the molecular literature says matters most
38958301.bottom_line: The current American guideline, which restates the 5 cm threshold, the 6-month decision point and the resect-all-men rule as conditional recommendations on low-quality evidence - and does so in 2024 without engaging the studies published since 2016 that found no threshold, showed six months to be too early, and showed the male diagnosis to be unreliable.
38958301.funding: No funding statement identified in the extracted HCA sections; flagged here as not established from the text rather than absent.

limitations: Retrospective multicentre design with non-standardised imaging protocols across sites
The authors note the score was validated internally only and requires external validation
Subtype assignment depended on locally performed immunohistochemistry of varying completeness
critique: The score is derived and validated in the same cohort, so AUROC 0.91 in 'validation' is an internal split, not independent performance; applied to a European case mix with a quarter the beta-catenin prevalence its positive predictive value would fall sharply

Industry funding from Bayer Korea is directly relevant: Bayer markets gadoxetic acid (Primovist), and the deliverable of this study is a contrast-enhanced MRI scoring system that increases the indication for that agent

Pathology-confirmed cases only, so the 26.1% beta-catenin figure is a resection and biopsy denominator; the striking male predominance may equally reflect which Korean patients get operated on as which develop adenomas
The 16.7% HCC rate in beta-catenin adenomas is cross-sectional co-occurrence at diagnosis, not observed transformation
Reported as patients and lesions interchangeably across analyses (121 vs 138), and subtype percentages are not stated as per-patient or per-lesion, making the denominators ambiguous

The finding that HCA was unsuspected in 31.6% of reports undermines the premise of any imaging-based pathway, including this paper's own score, yet it is not reconciled with the score's claimed accuracy
No size-stratified analysis of complications, so a cohort ideally placed to test the 5 cm threshold in a different epidemiological setting does not test it
39526315.bottom_line: Shows that in a low-contraceptive-use Asian population adenoma is far more often male and beta-catenin-activated than in Western series, which is a genuine challenge to guidelines built on European cohorts; but its imaging score is internally validated only and the study is funded by the manufacturer of the contrast agent it relies on.

limitations: Consensus guidance with no evidence base specific to benign tumours; the rarity of the indication precludes comparative data
The working group notes that categorisation requires individual case review rather than mechanical application
critique: An allocation document for a scarce resource with no stated outcome data behind its categories; the only relevant evidence - Chiche's three operative deaths and three fatal recurrences in 49 transplants, and Ziogas's 18.3% mortality in patients with a median MELD of 8 - is the kind of data that should inform these thresholds and is not visibly incorporated

Categorical algorithms applied to a condition this rare will determine individual access on the basis of expert judgement dressed as criteria, and the guidance concedes individual review is still needed - which makes the categories presentational

No definition of how adenoma size, number, subtype or prior intervention maps onto the categories is extractable from the text, so the document cannot be audited against the evidence on any of those variables

It gives no guidance on beta-catenin or sonic hedgehog status, the variables the molecular literature identifies as determining risk, so transplant access is governed by criteria that do not reference the biology

Fairness in allocation is the document's stated purpose, but transplanting a young patient with preserved liver function for a benign tumour has an opportunity cost in organs not offered to patients with liver failure, and no such comparison is presented
As national guidance it will be applied prospectively and uniformly despite resting on consensus alone, which is the strongest form of institutionalisation on the weakest form of evidence
40713471.bottom_line: UK national guidance assigning patients with benign liver tumours to four transplant-eligibility categories by consensus, with no cohort data and no reference to the molecular variables that determine adenoma risk - an allocation rule for a scarce resource institutionalised on expert opinion alone.
40713471.funding: No funding statement; produced by the NHSBT Liver Advisory Group Fair Transplant Working Group.

limitations: Only seven studies, which the authors say may itself account for the negligible heterogeneity
Non-uniform grading criteria for outcomes and moderate to severe risk of bias in most studies
Five studies reported a high number of interventions during follow-up, potentially retaining preferentially less aggressive HCAs in the surveillance group
Three studies had a high proportion of patients without baseline or follow-up imaging
Cohorts included men (8.1% pooled) and beta-catenin-mutated HCAs, populations that would not normally be surveilled, which the authors say would if anything overestimate malignant transformation
All subtypes pooled because subtype-stratified data were insufficient
Surgical pathology was unobtainable for all lesions, so some may have been focal nodular hyperplasia or may have harboured occult malignant foci
critique: The decisive flaw is the one the authors name but cannot repair: in five of seven studies lesions were pulled out of the surveillance group by intervention whenever they grew or looked worrying, so the pooled 0.5% bleeding and 0.8% transformation describe the lesions that were allowed to remain under observation - an informative-censoring problem that no random-effects model can correct

I2 of 0% across seven retrospective studies with four different size-change definitions is not evidence of consistency; with this few studies the heterogeneity statistic has almost no power, and the authors' own sensitivity analysis moving progression from 11.5% to 18.1% on removing one study shows the pooled estimate is fragile
The confidence interval for symptomatic bleeding runs from 0.1% to 3.5% - a 35-fold range - so the headline 'less than 1%' is far more precise-sounding than the underlying data support
Overlap with the depot's other papers is substantial (Barbier, Lammert, Klompenhouwer, Demory), so this meta-analysis is not independent evidence but a re-presentation of cohorts already counted
Pooling per-patient outcomes across studies that mixed solitary, multiple and adenomatosis cases, and that defined size change four different ways, produces a number without a coherent referent

The paper is written by radiologists and frames the conclusion as extending surveillance intervals, which is also the reading that maximises imaging utilisation; the alternative conclusion - that many of these patients need neither surgery nor indefinite imaging - is not examined
No assessment of publication bias was possible with seven studies, and the authors say so, but the direction of that bias in a surveillance literature is towards publishing cohorts that did well
41364225.bottom_line: The best current estimate of what happens to adenomas that are watched - 88.5% stable or regressing, symptomatic bleeding 0.5% and malignant transformation 0.8%, one to two orders of magnitude below the historical figures the 5 cm rule was built on - though informative censoring by intervention during follow-up means these are the outcomes of lesions permitted to stay under observation rather than of all adenomas over 5 cm.
41364225.funding: No datasets generated or analysed. 'The authors declare no competing interests.' No funding statement.

limitations: The authors note that no agent discussed has been tested clinically in hepatocellular adenoma
They acknowledge the rarity of the disease makes conventional trial design difficult
critique: Every therapeutic proposal in the review is hypothetical: there is no human efficacy or safety data for any named drug in hepatocellular adenoma, so the review describes a research agenda presented in the register of a treatment review
No systematic search, no quality appraisal, no explicit evidence grading, so a reader cannot tell which claims rest on preclinical data and which on analogy

Pathway-directed therapy presupposes molecular subtyping, which in turn presupposes biopsy or resection - the review does not address that the diagnostic prerequisite for its own proposals is what EASL declines to recommend routinely
Proposing immunosuppressive JAK inhibitors for a benign tumour in young women with a very low complication rate is a risk-benefit calculation the review does not perform
The journal's editor-in-chief is an author, which is disclosed but relevant to the editorial independence of a review with no new data

Natural history is the implicit comparator and is never quantified: given that most adenomas regress or remain stable without any treatment, the effect size any medical therapy would need to demonstrate is large and the review does not state it
41680345.bottom_line: Sets out a plausible subtype-matched research agenda for medical therapy of hepatocellular adenoma - GLP-1 agonists, JAK/STAT inhibitors, GLI1 antagonists - but contains no clinical data on any of them, so it establishes what might be tested rather than anything that can currently be offered.
41680345.funding: No funding. One author (JMC) is editor-in-chief of the journal.

limitations: Retrospective single-centre design
The authors note variable follow-up duration across the surveillance group
Subtype information was not available for every lesion
critique: All six malignant transformations occurring above 5 cm looks like support for the threshold, but every one was also beta-catenin-activated or inflammatory, so size and subtype are completely confounded in six events and the paper cannot separate them

Zero transformation in a surveillance group selected by clinicians who judged those lesions low-risk is the expected result of successful selection, not evidence that surveillance is safe for lesions they would not have selected
A 1.8% rupture rate across 164 patients means roughly three events; the figure is reassuring but imprecise
The 4-5 cm band finding (22.7% regression) is the most directly useful datum for the threshold debate and sits on about 11 of 44 patients

Regression in 18.4% is low compared with the 58.5% eventual regression in Klompenhouwer and the 69% in Lammert, which suggests either shorter follow-up or a stricter definition of regression; neither is stated in the reported results
No multivariable analysis, so none of the predictors can be adjusted for one another
Published 2026 but the recruitment period is not stated in the extracted text, so it is unclear whether management reflects current or historical practice
42214026.bottom_line: A contemporary surveillance-dominant cohort with very low rupture (1.8%) and no malignant transformation among watched patients, in which every HCC arose in a lesion that was both over 5 cm and of a high-risk subtype - so it is consistent with the threshold but cannot separate size from subtype in six events.
42214026.funding: No funding statement identified in the extracted text; flagged here as not established from the text rather than absent.

limitations: The authors state that germline predisposition in HCA remains poorly understood, with only MODY3/H-HCA, GSD/IHCA-B(I)HCA and FAP/B-HCA well characterised

They note that in unusual clinical scenarios (children, patients over 60, vascular liver disease) morphomolecular features become less well defined, overlap with focal nodular hyperplasia and the line defining malignancy blurs, with transformation more frequent
They concede no reliable routine immunohistochemical marker exists for SH-HCA
For HCC they note most genomic data come from resections of early-stage disease and may not capture advanced-disease biology
critique: Narrative review with no search strategy or quality appraisal; the quoted frequencies and complication rates are inherited from the same French and Korean series that generated the classification, so it is not independent corroboration

The two statements most relevant to a size threshold - that sonic hedgehog adenomas bleed below 5 cm and that exon 3 adenomas are resected whatever their size - are asserted as established practice without any cited cohort quantifying either, so the subtype-not-size argument here rests on expert assertion rather than data

Complication rates of 10-20% bleeding and 4-8% transformation are derived from resection series and are presented without that caveat, unlike the same group's 2022 review which states the bias explicitly

The classification it describes requires immunohistochemistry panels and, for sonic hedgehog and ambiguous GS patterns, molecular sequencing; the review does not address what a centre without these should do, which is where most 5 cm decisions are actually made
Subtype percentages differ from those in the same authors' 2022 review (shHCA 5-10% here vs 10% there; B-HCA 10% vs 11.2%) without explanation, illustrating how unstable these denominators are
The paper is largely about HCC; the HCA section is short and carries no numbers that a clinician could use to weigh resection against surveillance for a specific lesion
42678415.bottom_line: States the current WHO position that HCA management should follow subtype - with exon 3 beta-catenin adenomas resected regardless of size and sonic hedgehog adenomas bleeding below 5 cm - but as a narrative review it asserts this without new data, and concedes that the markers needed to identify the key subtypes are either insensitive, non-specific or available only by sequencing.
42678415.funding: National Research Foundation of Korea grant RS-2026-25468517 (YN Park). 'YN Park and C Sempoux have no competing interests to declare.'
